title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which AI-generated content, including deepfake images and fabricated text, was used to create a false news article depicting real, named public figures endorsing an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure did not occur inside a regulated AI product deployment but in the deliberate misuse of generative AI tools by bad actors to produce convincing fraudulent material. The scam exploited the surface credibility of professional-looking media content, placing the deception at the point where a potential investor encounters what appears to be legitimate financial journalism.

The mechanism depends on the gap between how convincing AI-generated content looks and how difficult it is for an ordinary reader to verify its origin. Catching it would have required either platform-level detection of synthetic media before distribution, or a reader who independently checked the Australian Financial Services licence register and confirmed that no such interview took place. ASIC's reported figures, a 182 percent rise in scams taken down and a 279 percent rise in phishing scams, indicate that this gap is being exploited at scale rather than in isolated cases.

What is not established is the identity of those responsible for the specific fake article, the number of people harmed by it, or the total financial losses attributable to this particular campaign.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article falsely depicted Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated story never actually occurred. This incident represents a growing trend of AI-generated scams that use deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to deceive investors. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows these sophisticated schemes are becoming increasingly prevalent and convincing.

ASIC reports taking down 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including a 279 percent jump in phishing scams and a 151 percent increase in fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated public figure, followed by other politicians and financial experts like Alan Kohler. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, websites, and advertisements to lure consumers. ASIC advises people to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that professional-looking content does not guarantee legitimacy.
